office.subject: reception
office.rationale: Reception is the first point of contact for visitors and must be the first space encountered after the main entry so visitors are greeted, oriented and registered before entering the rest of the building.
exceptions: Small coworking floors where badge-only access replaces a staffed desk
Buildings with a separate ground-floor lobby already serving reception

office.subject: visitor_waiting
office.rationale: Visitors are usually asked to wait near reception so that the host can collect them and so the receptionist can keep an eye on them; placing the waiting area out of sight of reception defeats both.
exceptions: Executive floors with a separate hosted lounge

office.subject: meeting_room
office.rationale: Meeting rooms are shared between teams, so they should open off common corridors or hubs rather than being reached through someone else's workspace, which disturbs that team each time a meeting convenes.
exceptions: Team-owned huddle rooms inside a neighbourhood

office.subject: focus_room
office.rationale: Focus or phone rooms are used for short bursts of concentrated work or calls taken from the open floor, so they lose their value if people have to walk far to reach one; clustering them around work neighbourhoods keeps them in use.
exceptions: Buildings where all enclosed rooms are bookable and centralised

office.subject: restroom
office.rationale: Restrooms must be reachable from the shared corridor network without passing through private offices, meeting rooms or work areas, both for privacy of the restroom user and for the people whose rooms would otherwise be traversed.

office.subject: restroom
office.rationale: A restroom door should not open directly onto a space where food is prepared, served or eaten, both for hygiene perception and for odour control; a short vestibule or separate corridor segment is the usual mitigation.
exceptions: Small single-user restrooms with a vestibule or airlock between them and the pantry

office.subject: floor
office.rationale: Each occupied tenant floor typically has at least one pantry or tea point so that coffee runs and lunch heating do not require riding lifts; this is a near-universal expectation for office fit-outs above a trivial headcount.
exceptions: Very small floors (under roughly 20 people) that share a pantry with a neighbouring floor
Mezzanine or technical floors

office.subject: server_room
office.rationale: Even a small office IT or comms room holds equipment and cabling that should not be casually accessible; it should sit behind a controlled door, usually reached from an IT or back-of-house zone rather than opening onto the public corridor.
exceptions: Micro-tenants whose single rack sits in a lockable cabinet rather than a dedicated room

office.subject: focus_room
office.rationale: Focus rooms and quiet work are hard to combine with a cafe or social hub, which generates conversation, blenders and foot traffic; placing them on opposite sides of a floor or with circulation between them reduces acoustic bleed.
exceptions: Floors that are entirely social, with no quiet programme

office.subject: open_workspace
office.rationale: Every occupied workspace needs a path to a protected egress stair within the travel distance allowed by life-safety rules; a work neighbourhood with no reachable stair is a programming failure before it is a code one.

office.subject: print_copy
office.rationale: Shared print and copy rooms serve multiple teams and generate noise and heat, so they belong off a corridor rather than inside a neighbourhood, which keeps traffic and sound out of work areas.
exceptions: Team-owned MFP alcoves within large neighbourhoods

office.subject: meeting_room
office.rationale: A meeting room reached only through someone's private office is effectively that person's room, which breaks the shared nature of meeting bookings and disrupts the office occupant each time.
exceptions: Executive suites where an adjoining meeting room is deliberately the executive's

office.subject: loading
office.rationale: Deliveries, waste and furniture moves should not cross the visitor experience at reception; a separate service entry or at minimum a different corridor keeps the two flows apart.
exceptions: Single-tenant buildings where a shared door handles both at off-peak times

office.subject: wellness_room
office.rationale: A wellness, mothers' or prayer room is used in moments of privacy and should not open directly off a busy work floor; a lockable door off a quieter corridor or support cluster is the common pattern.
exceptions: Small offices that genuinely have no private corner to spare

clinic.subject: reception
clinic.rationale: Patients arriving at an outpatient clinic must check in before being seen, and the check-in desk is the point at which triage and privacy procedures begin, so reception belongs at the public entry.

clinic.subject: patient_waiting
clinic.rationale: Patients wait where reception can see them, both so they can be called by name without walking a corridor and so staff can monitor the condition of anyone whose state might change while waiting.

clinic.subject: exam_room
clinic.rationale: Exam rooms are reached by both patients from the waiting area and clinicians from the staff core, so they open off a shared clinical corridor rather than another room; this also lets staff rotate between rooms efficiently.
exceptions: Dual-door exam rooms with separate patient and staff doors onto different corridors

clinic.subject: nurse_station
clinic.rationale: Nurses prepare patients, hand off samples and respond to calls from exam rooms, so the nurse station should be within a few steps of the exam rooms it supports rather than at the end of a corridor.
exceptions: Very small clinics where reception doubles as nurse station

clinic.subject: clean_supply
clinic.rationale: Clean supplies and soiled waste must not share a room or an adjacent door, to keep infectious materials away from sterile stock; typical practice places them on opposite segments of the staff corridor.

clinic.subject: staff_zone
clinic.rationale: Staff should be able to enter the clinical zone without crossing the patient waiting area, both for infection control and so clinicians are not waylaid before they have gowned up and reviewed the day's list.
exceptions: Micro-practices with one door for everyone

clinic.subject: patient_toilet
clinic.rationale: Patients often wait some time and may be asked to provide a sample, so a patient toilet reachable from the waiting area without passing through clinical space is standard; it also separates patient and staff restrooms.

clinic.subject: consult_room
clinic.rationale: Conversations in consult or exam rooms carry protected health information, so these rooms should not share a thin wall with the waiting area; a buffer corridor or a solid construction wall is normal practice.

clinic.subject: procedure_room
clinic.rationale: Patients coming out of a minor procedure are moved to a nearby recovery or observation bay before being discharged; placing recovery next to procedure keeps the transfer short and under staff view.
exceptions: Clinics that do no procedures and have no recovery programme

clinic.subject: lab_draw
clinic.rationale: Phlebotomy or sample-collection rooms are used by patients already in the clinical zone and by staff carrying samples to soiled utility or courier pickup; a position on the clinical corridor keeps both flows short.
exceptions: Clinics that send all lab work to an external drawing station

clinic.subject: medication_room
clinic.rationale: Controlled drug storage must be behind access-controlled staff doors and never open onto a space patients can enter unescorted; the medication room belongs on the staff side of the clinical corridor.

clinic.subject: staff_respite
clinic.rationale: Staff lounges and respite rooms need acoustic and visual separation from patients, both so staff can decompress and so patients do not see clinicians eating or on the phone; placing them in the staff zone solves both.

clinic.subject: public_entry
clinic.rationale: An accessible route from the public entry to reception, waiting and at least one exam room is a baseline programmatic requirement, independent of local code specifics; if the graph cannot route a wheelchair, the plan is wrong.

clinic.subject: soiled_utility
clinic.rationale: Soiled waste and linens leave the clinic through a service route rather than through patient areas, so the soiled utility should sit on a path that reaches a back-of-house exit without entering waiting or clinical corridors.
exceptions: Very small clinics that bag waste for pickup at the main door after hours

hospital.subject: emergency_department
hospital.rationale: An emergency department needs a dedicated ambulance entry separate from the walk-in entry so that stretcher-borne patients bypass the triage queue and go directly to a resuscitation bay; combining the two bottlenecks both flows.
exceptions: Rural critical-access hospitals with very low volumes

hospital.subject: triage
hospital.rationale: Walk-in patients must be assessed by a triage nurse before being placed in the waiting area so that time-critical conditions are identified; the triage desk is therefore the first space inside the walk-in door.

hospital.subject: resuscitation_bay
hospital.rationale: Resuscitation bays receive patients from ambulance offload within seconds, so they open directly off the ambulance entry; placing any other room between them costs life-critical time.

hospital.subject: operating_room
hospital.rationale: Operating rooms sit inside a restricted sterile zone with its own gowning and scrub rooms; entry from a general hospital corridor would defeat the staged cleanliness that surgical safety depends on.

hospital.subject: clean_core
hospital.rationale: Around operating rooms, clean supplies and soiled materials travel on separate corridors so that used instruments and dirty linen never cross packs coming from sterile processing; this is often shown as a two-corridor or racetrack layout.
exceptions: Older hospitals retrofitted with single-corridor ORs and strict procedural separation

hospital.subject: intensive_care
hospital.rationale: Post-surgical patients who need intensive care are transported from the OR to the ICU, so placing them on the same floor or a direct vertical link reduces the risk of in-transit deterioration.
exceptions: Hospitals with a dedicated post-anaesthesia care unit that bridges OR and ICU

hospital.subject: inpatient_ward
hospital.rationale: Inpatient wards are reached through a controlled visitor route with its own lifts or vestibule, not directly off the main public lobby, so that visitor flow can be managed, infectious outbreaks contained and after-hours access limited.

hospital.subject: isolation_room
hospital.rationale: Airborne-isolation rooms need an anteroom to buffer pressure between the corridor and the patient room; without it, opening the door breaks the pressure regime that protects staff and other patients.
exceptions: Droplet-only isolation rooms where the local code does not require an anteroom

hospital.subject: nurse_station
hospital.rationale: Nurses must be able to see or quickly reach the patient rooms they monitor, so each station serves a cluster of rooms within a short walking distance; decentralised stations are increasingly used for exactly this reason.

hospital.subject: imaging
hospital.rationale: Emergency patients are frequent users of imaging, especially CT, so placing imaging on the same level and near the ED keeps stretcher transports short; otherwise the ED spends staff on escorts.
exceptions: Hospitals with ED-dedicated imaging inside the department

hospital.subject: pharmacy
hospital.rationale: Central pharmacy holds controlled substances and large stocks of medication; access is through staff-only doors and ideally not visible from public circulation, both for security and for the quiet needed during compounding.
exceptions: Outpatient dispensing windows, which are a separate programme that does front the public

hospital.subject: morgue
hospital.rationale: Deceased patients are moved from the morgue to a service exit without crossing public or patient areas; the route uses service lifts and back-of-house corridors for dignity and infection control.

hospital.subject: loading_dock
hospital.rationale: Supplies for sterile processing and the OR arrive at the loading dock and must reach storage through a service route that does not cross clinical corridors, to keep packaging dirt and cardboard out of clinical zones.

hospital.subject: public_waiting
hospital.rationale: Visitors in public waiting should not reach clinical corridors without passing through a controlled door; otherwise visitors wander into treatment areas and privacy and infection control both break down.

hospital.subject: outpatient_exam_room
hospital.rationale: Outpatient exam rooms in a hospital's clinic wing open off a shared clinical corridor rather than another room, so that both patients called from waiting and clinicians moving between rooms reach them without crossing unrelated treatment spaces.
exceptions: Dual-door exam rooms with a separate patient door off a sub-waiting and a staff door off the clean corridor

hospital.subject: outpatient_sub_waiting
hospital.rationale: Large outpatient clinics break the main waiting area into sub-waiting pods next to each exam-room cluster so that walking distance from called patient to room stays short and the main lobby does not have to seat every department's load at once.
exceptions: Small clinics inside a hospital that share the main outpatient waiting hall

hospital.subject: outpatient_clean_supply
hospital.rationale: Within an outpatient module, the clean supply room and the soiled utility room sit on separated segments of the staff corridor so that stocked packs and used instruments never share a door or an adjacent wall; this is the same clean-and-dirty rule as the OR side applied at clinic scale.

hospital.subject: outpatient_consult_room
hospital.rationale: Consult rooms where a clinician discusses results or a diagnosis should not open directly onto the public waiting area, both because conversations carry protected health information through the door each time it opens and because waiting patients can see who is consulted next.
exceptions: Sub-waiting pods where the consult-room door opens onto a small vestibule segment rather than the main waiting hall

datacenter.subject: mantrap
datacenter.rationale: A mantrap or airlock vestibule with interlocked doors is the sole personnel path from the building entry into the secure zone; tailgating is a standard attack and the mantrap forces one person per transit.
exceptions: Very small co-located cages where the cage itself acts as the controlled boundary

datacenter.subject: data_hall
datacenter.rationale: The data hall must not be reachable from any route that has not passed the mantrap; otherwise the mantrap is bypassable and the physical security model is broken.

datacenter.subject: electrical_room
datacenter.rationale: Power distribution rooms sit next to the data halls they feed to keep busway or cable runs short, limit voltage drop and losses, and reduce the floor area given over to electrical routing.

datacenter.subject: mechanical_room
datacenter.rationale: Cooling plant and air handlers sit immediately adjacent to the data halls they cool, usually on at least two sides, so that duct and piping runs are short and airflow paths are predictable.
exceptions: Rooftop or yard-based cooling plant connected through risers

datacenter.subject: data_hall
datacenter.rationale: Any data hall above the smallest tier is fed by at least two independent electrical paths (A and B) so that maintenance or failure of one does not drop the load; this shapes the number and placement of electrical rooms.
exceptions: Tier I facilities that explicitly accept single-path risk

datacenter.subject: electrical_path_a
datacenter.rationale: The A and B electrical paths run in separate rooms and separate riser shafts so that a fire, flood or physical incident in one path cannot take out the other; shared rooms defeat the redundancy the design claims.

datacenter.subject: data_hall
datacenter.rationale: Cooling, like power, is served by concurrently maintainable paths so that a chiller or CRAH outage does not raise hall temperatures; the mechanical rooms and piping are duplicated and physically separated.
exceptions: Tier I facilities that accept single-path cooling risk

datacenter.subject: generator_yard
datacenter.rationale: Backup generators and their bulk fuel storage are usually in separated enclosures with fire-rated construction between them, so that a generator fire does not involve the fuel farm; day tanks adjacent to generators are a different case.
exceptions: Small installations with integrated sub-base tanks on each generator

datacenter.subject: loading_dock
datacenter.rationale: Equipment arrives at the loading dock and must reach the data halls through a service corridor wide enough for pallets and racks, usually without passing through electrical or mechanical rooms; this corridor is deliberately short.

datacenter.subject: staging
datacenter.rationale: Incoming servers are unpacked, inspected and configured in a staging or build room before being rolled into the data hall, so that packaging material and uncontrolled devices never enter the production environment.
exceptions: Co-location sites where customers bring pre-built racks

datacenter.subject: network_operations_center
datacenter.rationale: Operators sit in a NOC with HVAC tuned for people, not for racks, so the NOC is a separate room from the data hall itself, usually with glass that lets staff see the floor without being in it.
exceptions: Small sites where a single desk inside the hall acts as the NOC

datacenter.subject: meet_me_room
datacenter.rationale: Carrier handoff and cross-connect rooms sit on the edge of the data hall so that fibre runs between carriers and customer cages stay short and manageable; placing them far away inflates cabling and latency budgets.
exceptions: Hyperscale sites with a different carrier handoff model

datacenter.subject: security_room
datacenter.rationale: A staffed security office sits next to the mantrap so that guards can visually verify entrants, respond to alarms and manage overrides; a remote-only guard station undermines the point of the mantrap.
exceptions: Remote-managed sites with no onsite guards, which accept the trade-off

datacenter.subject: office
datacenter.rationale: Administrative offices sit on the public side of the mantrap, not inside the secure zone; mixing them weakens access control and forces office visitors to be processed as data-hall visitors.

airport.subject: landside
airport.rationale: The entire terminal is split into a landside that anyone may enter and an airside reached only through security screening; this split is the defining geometric constraint of a passenger terminal.

airport.subject: security_screening
airport.rationale: Security screening is the only path from landside to airside; a passenger who reaches the airside without passing screening breaks the security model of the airport.

airport.subject: check_in
airport.rationale: Check-in and bag drop sit on landside near the terminal entry so that passengers process bags before approaching security; placing check-in airside would require the airport to clear passengers before their baggage is accepted.
exceptions: Fully off-airport check-in in some rail-integrated systems

airport.subject: check_in
airport.rationale: Passengers reach check-in from landside circulation and then move to security; routing the flow in the reverse order makes no operational sense and is not how terminals are planned.

airport.subject: departure_gate
airport.rationale: Departure gates sit on the airside concourse and are reached from it; placing them on landside would mean passengers board without being screened, which the airport cannot permit.

airport.subject: arrivals
airport.rationale: Arriving and departing passengers are kept apart, often on different levels, so that arrivals, especially international ones awaiting immigration, do not mix with screened departing passengers and defeat security.
exceptions: Very small regional terminals with procedural separation in time rather than space

airport.subject: international_arrivals
airport.rationale: International arriving passengers pass through immigration before reaching baggage reclaim, so that only admitted passengers can collect bags and proceed to customs; the gate-to-immigration-to-baggage order is near-universal.
exceptions: Pre-clearance arrangements that move immigration to the origin airport

airport.subject: customs
airport.rationale: Customs is positioned after baggage reclaim so passengers present with their bags; placing customs before reclaim would require declaring goods the passenger has not yet collected.

airport.subject: baggage_handling
airport.rationale: The baggage handling system sits directly behind the check-in counters so that bags tagged at check-in drop immediately onto the sortation conveyors; a long landside bag path adds cost, risk and mis-sorts.

airport.subject: baggage_reclaim
airport.rationale: Baggage reclaim sits on the boundary between the sterile arrivals corridor and the landside meeters-and-greeters area, so that passengers pick up bags and exit to landside in one move.

airport.subject: concessions
airport.rationale: Retail and food concessions are concentrated airside, after security, because that is where departing passengers have time to dwell; concentrating them landside would waste the captive audience.
exceptions: Landside meeters' halls which still have some retail aimed at non-travellers

airport.subject: airside_concourse
airport.rationale: Each airside concourse needs restrooms within a short walk of every gate, because passengers may spend hours airside and because gate-hold rooms are not supposed to double as waiting-for-toilet queues.

airport.subject: staff_route
airport.rationale: Staff who have not cleared passenger screening must not share a corridor with arriving passengers between the gate and immigration, to keep the sterile arrivals corridor sterile; staff use separate doors and lifts.

airport.subject: apron_access
airport.rationale: The airside apron, where aircraft park and are serviced, is reachable only through controlled doors on the airside; a door that connects landside directly to the apron is a security breach of the terminal.
